item.title: Confapi Varese-AVSI agreement for youth training
item.description: Protocol signed on 17 September between Confapi Varese and the AVSI Foundation to train young people through apprenticeships and dual training.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Signed protocol between Confapi Varese and Fondazione AVSI - Objective: train young people through apprenticeship and dual training - Signing took place on September 17 at the Lodovico Pogliaghi House Museum
## Key facts - Signing entity: Confapi Varese - Signing entity: Fondazione AVSI - Signing date: September 17 - Location: Lodovico Pogliaghi House Museum - Parties involved: Marco Tenaglia, Giorgio Capitanio, Roberto Di Francesco
On September 17, in the evocative setting of the Lodovico Pogliaghi House Museum in Santa Maria del Monte, a new memorandum of understanding was signed between Confapi Varese and Fondazione AVSI. The event, part of the benefit evening entitled ‘On the Notes of Varese, Rio and the World’, saw the participation of prominent figures from the two organizations, called upon to formalize a joint commitment aimed at creating a bridge between young people in reception pathways and the productive fabric of small and medium-sized enterprises in the Varese area. The evening was further enriched by the artistic performances of soprano Fernanda Schleder and baritone Frederico de Assis, coming from the Rio de Janeiro Opera Theatre, creating a blend of culture and social purpose.
### Strategic objectives of the protocol The signing of the document, affixed by Marco Tenaglia for Confapi Varese and by Giorgio Capitanio, AVSI Europe Regional Manager, marks the formal start of an operational collaboration. The primary intent is to structure a pathway that combines reception, training and job placement. Fondazione AVSI, leveraging the network of Families for Reception that follows young people in their personal development, will be responsible for identifying profiles ready for the labour market. Confapi Varese, for its part, will deploy its services dedicated to apprenticeship, involving the extensive network of associated small and medium-sized industries. The aim is to effectively meet the professional skill needs of companies, while at the same time offering young people a concrete channel to achieve professional autonomy. This synergy aims to turn corporate social responsibility into an established practice, capable of generating measurable benefits both for companies and for the local Varese community. The agreement fits into an economic landscape in which, according to the source, one out of two companies records serious difficulties in finding the professional figures it needs for its productive activities. The initiative is not limited to a mere programmatic intent, but translates into an operational model based on dual training, which facilitates the insertion of young people into the productive system. The involvement of Api Servizi alle Imprese, in the person of its CEO Roberto Di Francesco, guarantees the provision of specific know-how in training and apprenticeship, essential for building tailor-made paths that respond to the real needs of the small and medium-sized enterprises associated with Confapi.
### Integration and value of work The president of Confapi Varese, Marco Tenaglia, stressed that the ultimate goal is to look to the future, laying the foundations for an authentic and structured integration. The outlined path is based on three fundamental pillars: training, welcome, and cultural value. These components, if correctly integrated, are able to produce tangible benefits both for the young people involved and for the country as a whole. The structure of the agreement provides for a clear distinction of operational competencies: AVSI manages the accompaniment and preparation phase of the young people through its widespread network, while Confapi Varese coordinates the technical phase of job insertion. This systemic approach aims to bridge the gap between the demand for technical skills from companies and the training offer, seeking to make the job insertion process a smooth and well-oiled mechanism capable of enhancing the potential of each young participant in the program. Attention to dual training represents, in this sense, the response to a shortage of professional figures that penalizes not only large industries, but especially the small realities that constitute the economic backbone of the Varese territory.

Per le imprese del territorio interessate ad aderire a questo modello di inserimento, il primo passo operativo consiste nel rivolgersi alla struttura tecnica di Confapi Varese, che attraverso i propri servizi dedicati all'apprendistato, coordina le richieste di formazione duale. Le aziende possono richiedere informazioni direttamente al servizio di Api Servizi alle Imprese per comprendere come strutturare percorsi di inserimento che siano in linea con le competenze ricercate e con le finalità del protocollo sottoscritto con AVSI. La collaborazione mira a fornire alle PMI le competenze necessarie per formare internamente i giovani, riducendo il tempo di ricerca del personale e garantendo una crescita professionale monitorata e strutturata secondo le esigenze produttive del comparto industriale di riferimento.
### Come procedere per le aziende Le realtà interessate devono valutare la propria disponibilità ad accogliere giovani in apprendistato, verificando la compatibilità con i programmi di formazione duale previsti dal protocollo. Il processo prevede una fase di analisi delle competenze necessarie in azienda, seguita da un matching con i giovani individuati da Fondazione AVSI. Per le imprese che desiderano approfondire i meccanismi di gestione del personale e delle assunzioni, è possibile consultare i dati relativi al proprio settore di riferimento o esplorare le opportunità di inserimento attraverso i canali ufficiali dell'associazione. Chi fosse interessato a monitorare costantemente le opportunità di networking o le iniziative di formazione nel settore, può far riferimento alle guide e agli strumenti disponibili per orientarsi nel mercato del lavoro, come quelli consultabili tramite il portale [annunci lavoro](nav:jobs). La struttura del protocollo garantisce un accompagnamento continuo, assicurando che l'inserimento non sia solo un momento di assunzione, ma un percorso di crescita che risponda alle sfide di un mercato del lavoro dinamico e sempre più esigente in termini di specializzazione tecnica.

item.title: Frontiersmen, Malesco writes to the Government for funds
item.description: Enrico Barbazza, mayor of Malesco, requests the Government to fully transfer the resources allocated to border municipalities to support local services.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The mayor of Malesco demands the full transfer of cross-border resources. - Enrico Barbazza writes to the Government to defend funds allocated to the territories. - An immediate discussion between local institutions and the national Government has been requested. - These resources are essential for services, road networks, and municipal security.
## Key facts - Promoter: Enrico Barbazza, Mayor of Malesco - Recipients: Prime Minister, Ministers of Economy/Interior, Parliamentarians - Objective: Full transfer of resources to border municipalities - Motivation: Support for local services, road networks, and infrastructure
Enrico Barbazza, mayor of Malesco, has formalized an urgent request addressed to the highest offices of the Italian State, including the President of the Council of Ministers, the Minister of Economy and Finance, and the Minister of the Interior, as well as parliamentarians from border regions. The letter aims to raise the issue regarding the defense of financial resources derived from cross-border labor, which are allocated to border municipalities according to current regulations. The mayor of Malesco emphasizes that these funds do not represent a discretionary concession, but rather a resource linked to an economic and social phenomenon that daily impacts thousands of workers and their families. The central point raised is the need to guarantee the full transfer of the sums due to local administrations, which are on the front line in managing the effects of international mobility.
### The role of border municipalities Local administrations located along the border play a fundamental role in the stability of the system. Without the resources derived from cross-border work, municipalities risk being unable to adequately guarantee essential services such as land maintenance, security, road networks, transport, and social services. Mayor Barbazza highlights how the border condition entails specific burdens that local communities have been concretely supporting for years. The concern expressed in the letter regards the risk that any decisions aimed at withholding or reducing these sums could severely penalize the territories involved. The request to the Government is clear: respect the commitments made and ensure certainty of the rules, avoiding that the burden of public finance be offloaded onto small municipalities. [Discover the dynamics of cross-border work](nav:jobs). The issue raised by Enrico Barbazza highlights the financial fragility of border municipalities, where the presence of a large number of workers employed in Switzerland places constant pressure on public services. A practical analysis of this situation shows how territory management in cross-border areas requires higher investments compared to inland zones, due to the need to manage intense commuter flows passing through crossings such as Brogeda or Gaggiolo. The concern of mayors, as expressed by the representative of Malesco, does not only concern the present, but the long-term sustainability of local infrastructure. If the resources allocated to municipalities were reduced, we would witness a deterioration in the quality of life for resident citizens and for the cross-border workers themselves who experience the territory on a daily basis.
### Scenarios and local impacts The feared risk is a disproportion between the management responsibilities of municipalities and the resources actually available. Border municipalities, in fact, must not only guarantee ordinary services but must also address specific needs related to the international mobility that characterizes the daily life of workers. The requested discussion with the Government is intended precisely to prevent resources from being considered as a 'nest egg' to be held centrally, rather than as funds intended to compensate for the administrative and social workload sustained locally. For a cross-border worker, seeing their municipality of residence in difficulty means, indirectly, seeing a decrease in the quality of services that they and their family benefit from. It is a matter of institutional equity: resources linked to cross-border work must return to the territories that bear the burden of the border on a daily basis. The invitation to the Government is to open a transparent dialogue table, capable of recognizing that the border cannot be considered an administrative boundary only when it comes to supporting territories, only to be forgotten when it comes to allocating resources. item.title: Swiss Border Study: Border Costs and Collapse
item.description: Federal Council report and Ecoplan study: traffic jams for 422,000 hours a day, billion-dollar costs and the collapse of border workers by up to 60% without Schengen.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Federal Council report published on September 18, 2026. - Swiss GDP contraction of up to 3.9% in the event of leaving Schengen. - Annual income loss of up to 1,293 / 1,300 francs per inhabitant. - Collapse of cross-border workers estimated at up to 60%.
## Key facts - Report date: September 18, 2026 - Study conducted by: Ecoplan - Study commissioner: Federal Office of Justice - Expected GDP contraction: Up to 3.9% - Per capita income loss: Up to 1,293 / 1,300 francs per year - Hours lost per day in traffic queues: 422,000 hours - Annual commuting costs: Between 1.08 and 2.27 billion francs
Association with the European Schengen and Dublin agreements guarantees Switzerland enormous economic and internal security advantages, as clearly confirmed by the Federal Council report, adopted on September 18, 2026 on the basis of an analytical study conducted by Ecoplan on behalf of the Federal Office of Justice. The analysis outlines a detailed picture of the socio-economic impacts if Switzerland were to abandon the agreements with the European Union, highlighting price increases, infrastructure paralysis, and severe penalties for border regions such as Canton Ticino. The forecasting data projected to 2035 show scenarios of severe recession in the most unfavorable scenario, including a contraction of Swiss Gross Domestic Product that could suffer a reduction of up to 3.9%. This economic contraction would translate into an income drop of up to 1,293 / 1,300 francs per year per inhabitant. Tourism would also suffer a severe crisis, as the need to apply for a separate Swiss visa would discourage non-EU tourists, with estimated losses for the tourism sector fluctuating between 320 and 810 million francs per year. The lack of fluidity at the border would make the Swiss economic hub less attractive and less competitive on a global scale.
### Economic and tourism scenarios by 2035 Economic projections highlight how the potential abandonment of the European bilateral agreements would create a situation of severe financial instability for the entire Swiss economy. The loss of attractiveness of the economic hub would directly reflect on international markets and Switzerland's ability to attract capital and talent. The tourism sector, in particular, would suffer a very hard blow due to bureaucratic barriers for travelers from third countries, with negative impacts on hotels, restaurants, and related industries. The estimate of losses between 320 and 810 million francs per year captures the vulnerability of a sector heavily dependent on free movement and ease of access to Swiss territory. These dynamics demonstrate how closely the economic stability of the Confederation is tied to the Schengen and Dublin agreements, whose potential termination would trigger a chain reaction capable of hitting every single productive sector, from major financial centers to peripheral and border regions like Canton Ticino, which would bear the brunt of the consequences of a rigid and barely permeable border for goods, services, and people. Without the Schengen Agreement, the border crossings between Switzerland and neighboring countries, including Italy, France, Germany, and Austria, would effectively become external borders of the European Union. This would impose systematic checks on people both entering and exiting, radically altering the daily mobility of workers and citizens. For highly integrated territories such as the Canton of Ticino, Geneva, and Basel, the daily consequences would be immediate and disruptive. The report estimates as many as 422,000 hours lost per day: this is the time commuters would spend stuck in traffic jams at border crossings such as Chiasso, Stabio, or Ponte Tresa on every single working day. In addition to this, travel costs related to delays and traffic would amount to between 1.08 and 2.27 billion Swiss francs per year.
### Impact on mobility and the real estate market The disproportionate increase in waiting times at border crossings could lead to a collapse in cross-border workers, with an estimated reduction of up to 60% in the total number of people crossing the border daily for work. Key sectors such as healthcare, specifically regarding care services, and the restaurant industry would risk total paralysis due to a severe labor shortage. Furthermore, the effects would be heavily felt on the region's real estate market: it is estimated that up to 170,000 people could decide to transfer their residence directly to Switzerland to avoid daily checks and endless queues at the border. This shift in residents would alter demographic balances and housing demand both in Swiss territory and in the Italian border areas, generating tensions on property prices and rents. To understand the magnitude of such transformations, one must consider [border waiting times](nav:border) as a key indicator of cross-border economic fluidity, where every slowdown translates into very high operating costs for companies and a drastic deterioration in the quality of life of commuters who travel daily between Italy and Switzerland for professional reasons.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). Beyond strictly financial and mobility aspects, the Federal Council's report emphasizes the invaluable importance of police cooperation and the management of migratory flows through the European system. In 2025 alone, thanks to the Schengen Information System, Swiss law enforcement recorded approximately 40,000 relevant hits, promptly identifying criminals and dangerous individuals. Without access to this shared database, Switzerland would not be able to guarantee the same security standards, not even by increasing its domestic investments. On the asylum front, exiting the Dublin system would prevent Switzerland from transferring asylum seekers to the first EU entry country. The obligation to examine all applications on its own territory would prolong stay durations, leading to an estimated cost increase between 166 and 824 million francs.
### Why hypothetical savings are not enough The report clarifies a fundamental misunderstanding regarding the alleged financial benefits of a potential exit: any savings resulting from the cessation of contributions paid to the EU for the management of Schengen and Dublin would by no means cover the costs necessary to reintroduce and manage comprehensive border controls, hire new border personnel, upgrade road and customs infrastructure, as well as create and maintain proprietary security databases. item.title: Border taxes Italy Switzerland 2026: driving over 20 km
item.description: Tax rules 2026 for border workers over 20 km: source tax, deductibles of 7,500 or 10,000 euros and double taxation management.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Withholding tax levied only in Switzerland - Exemptions: 7,500 euros (old) or 10,000 euros (new) - New Agreement in force since January 1, 2024 - Tax credit in Italy to avoid double taxation
## Key facts Frontalieri Agreement: signed 12/23/2020, in force 01/01/2024 Italian Ratification: Law 83 of 06/13/2023 Double Taxation Convention: 12/09/1976 Exemption for New Frontalieri: 10,000 euros Exemption for Old Frontalieri: 7,500 euros IRPEF 23%: up to 28,000 euros
The tax framework for those who work in Switzerland and reside in Italy is governed by precise rules, with particular attention to those who exceed a distance of 20 km. The withholding tax on employment income is levied exclusively in Switzerland. To prevent the worker from paying twice on the same income, Italy applies a tax credit through the CE section of the 730 tax return.
### The new tax regime The New Frontalieri Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020, and ratified in Italy with Law 83 of June 13, 2023, entered into force on January 1, 2024. This text defines the basis of current taxation, which will continue through 2026. Since Switzerland is not a member of the EU or EEA, it relies on the Double Taxation Convention signed on December 9, 1976, to coordinate tax flows with the Italian State.
The administration of these taxes is divided between the AFC/ESTV (Federal Tax Administration) at the federal level and the cantonal tax administrations. It is important to clarify that entities such as UFAS or BFS have no power to set tax rates, as they deal respectively with social security and statistics. Workers who acquired frontier worker status before July 17, 2023, benefit from a transitional regime valid until 2033, with an exemption of 7,500 euros, while new entries have an exemption of 10,000 euros. ## Practical Analysis and Tax Scenarios The distinction between cross-border workers residing at different distances from the border, particularly the 20 km limit, influences the perception of the overall tax burden. Although withholding tax is collected in Switzerland, the final calculation in Italy depends on IRPEF rates: 23% for income up to 28,000 euros, 35% between 28,001 and 50,000 euros, and 43% over 50,000 euros.
### Hypothetical Taxation Scenarios To understand the impact, let us consider two scenarios based on the provided exemptions. In a first hypothetical scenario, an 'old' cross-border worker (active before July 17, 2023) applies an exemption of 7,500 euros to their income before calculating the tax impact in Italy. In a second scenario, a 'new' cross-border worker can benefit from the higher exemption of 10,000 euros.
The analysis of the net amount also depends on mandatory Swiss contributions. The payslip shows AVS/AI/IPG deductions at 5.3% borne by the employee, unemployment insurance AD/AC at 1.1% (with a ceiling of 148,200 CHF), and LAINF between 0.7% and 1.5%. To these is added the LPP, which varies between 7% and 18% depending on the age group, starting from age 25.
The comparison between the two regimes shows how the 2024-2033 transitional regime protects long-term workers, while new agreements seek to standardize exemption thresholds. Those residing beyond 20 km must carefully monitor the tax credit to avoid reporting errors that could lead to penalties from the Agenzia delle Entrate. To optimize the calculation of your net salary, it is useful to use a [calculator](nav:calculator) updated with the 2026 rates.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ## Operational Guide and Steps to Follow To correctly manage taxation in 2026, especially for those residing beyond 20 km, it is necessary to follow a rigorous reporting procedure. Managing the flows between Switzerland and Italy requires precision in the documents submitted to the Agenzia delle Entrate and the MEF.
### Tax Declaration Checklist 1. Retrieval of the Swiss income certificate: a fundamental document issued by the cantonal tax administration. 2. Verification of the applicable exemption: determine whether you fall under the 'old cross-border commuters' (7,500 euro exemption) or the 'new' ones (10,000 euro exemption). 3. Completion of the CE section of the 730 form: entry of taxes paid in Switzerland to request the tax credit and neutralize double taxation. 4. Check of social security contributions: verification of AVS and LPP quotas paid for possible coordination with INPS.
In addition to taxes, the cross-border worker must manage the LAMal health insurance. Holders of a G permit have a right of option for insurance; for adults, the provided deductibles vary from 300 to 2,500 CHF. It is essential that this choice is consistent with one's health situation and budget.

The implementation of the initiative proposed by the SVP would have direct and heavy repercussions on daily mobility. According to the Federal Council's analyses, Switzerland records approximately 2.2 million border crossings every day. This massive flow, which includes several hundred thousand cross-border commuters, would be overturned by permanent and systematic controls.
### Congestion and traffic costs
The introduction of a complete presence at border crossings would generate what the Government defines as strong pressure on the economy and on commuter traffic. In particular, border areas would suffer a devastating impact due to what would be defined as a congestion cost of billions of francs. This scenario concerns not only the time lost in slowdowns, but the entire economic impact resulting from the inefficiency of border flows.
The Executive also emphasizes that increasing the personnel assigned to border protection would entail high costs, adding a further burden to public coffers. In addition to the direct charges, the risk of compromising well-being in Switzerland is one of the Government's central concerns, which sees this measure as a threat to the country's economic stability.
### The risk to internal security
Contrary to what is claimed by the promoters, the Federal Council believes that systematic controls would not be suitable instruments to curb secondary migration or cross-border crime. The Government reiterates that the current customs system already carries out controls based on the situation and risks, which can be intensified if necessary, without however blocking the entire circulation system.
Another critical point concerns access to data. If Switzerland were to abandon the Schengen/Dublin system to implement the initiative, it would lose access to European research databases. This weakening of international cooperation would lead to a concrete threat to internal security, making it more difficult to monitor flows and manage cross-border threats. The act, made known through a direct note from the MEF, represents the definitive turning point for the funding of Italian territories located adjacent to Switzerland. The objective is to provide economic resources to those populated centers that, due to their geographical position, manage the complexities related to the constant flow of cross-border workers and residents. The funds necessary for the disbursement are drawn from the Fund for the economic development of border territories, an institution created specifically to mitigate disparities and strengthen marginal areas.
The allocation of resources follows precise geographical criteria. To be considered beneficiaries, Municipalities must be located within a radius of 20 kilometers from the border line. The scope is further defined based on the bordering Swiss territories: the benefit indeed concerns Italian municipalities bordering the Cantons of Ticino, Graubünden, and Valais. This perimeter ensures that the funds reach exactly where the impact of commuting is most pronounced, ensuring that local administrations have the means to manage the infrastructural friction generated by daily flows towards Switzerland. ## Implicazioni per l'area di frontiera L'erogazione di questi fondi ha un impatto diretto sulla qualità della vita di chi attraversa ogni giorno il confine. item.title: Psychic absences in Ticino: 51% end up in dismissal
item.description: In Ticino, 51% of absences due to mental causes lead to the dissolution of the contract. The share of AI beneficiaries for psychiatric reasons rose to 51%.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - 51% of absences due to mental illness in Ticino ends with the termination of the contract - 51% of AI pension recipients in Ticino have psychiatric reasons, compared to 33% twentyyears ago - Absenteeism should be considered a symptom, not the problem itself
- Percentage of mental absences that end in the dissolution of the contract: 51% - Share of AI beneficiaries for psychiatric reasons in Ticino: 51% - Share twentyyears ago: 33% - Priority of Swiss disability insurance: professional reintegration
In 51% of cases, an absence from work related to a mental illness ends with the termination of the contract. And still 51% represents today, in Ticino, the share of beneficiaries of an AI pension for psychiatric reasons, compared to 33% just over twentyyears ago. Two numbers that show how mental discomfort has become one of the central issues in the world of work.
The theme was at the center of a conference organized in Mendrisio da Compasso, where it emerged that mental health is less and less a taboo, but where the early recognition of signs of difficulty remains crucial.
"You lose contacts, you lose the habit of working," Marzio Proietti, vice president of Compasso, explains to the RSI Newspaper. For this reason, he stresses, it is important to encourage a gradual return, without putting pressure on the employee and also providing for trial periods.
### The Role of Disability Insurance
The logic of ## Practical analysis: what changes for workers and companies
The two key figures — 51% of contract terminations due to mental health absences and 51% of disability insurance beneficiaries for psychiatric reasons — are no coincidence. They represent a significant increase compared to the 33% recorded twenty years ago, indicating that mental distress is becoming a central issue in the Swiss labor market.
### The human and business cost
The cost is not only for those who suffer: we companies risk losing collaborators, experience, and skills. And when an absence is prolonged, the chances of an effective reintegration decrease. This is particularly relevant for cross-border workers, who commute daily between Italy and Switzerland, where every day of absence can compromise the work routine.
For workers with G or B permits, prolonged absenteeism can have direct consequences on access to the LAMal health insurance and disability insurance coverage. Early recognition of signals therefore becomes a systemic issue, not just an individual one.
### Risk factors and burnout
The factors that can foster stress conditions up to burnout are varied: lack of recognition and appreciation, a difficult relationship with superiors or colleagues, a non-serene work environment, and the absence of a clear separation between professional and private life. According to Renato Dotti, president of the Forum Gestione Salute in Azienda, leadership is needed that is first and foremost capable of listening to the needs of collaborators.
This means building a 'positive environment' and creating that psychological safety that allows people to express their discomfort, but also to talk about mistakes without feeling immediately exposed or judged. For cross-border workers, often subject to double stress (work and cross-border family life), this safety is fundamental.
### The before and after comparison
Twenty years ago, 33% of disability pension beneficiaries had psychiatric reasons. Today that 33% has become 51%. This shift indicates that the Swiss healthcare and social security system is experiencing an exponential growth in cases related to mental health. For companies, intervening before a situation of vulnerability turns into a long absence means not only saving skills but also reducing absenteeism costs.
A structured approach — with gradual returns, probation periods, and active listening — can produce benefits for both parties: 'The employer does not lose the skills of their collaborator and the worker does not lose their job'.

item.title: Seizure of protected parrots at the Gandria crossing
item.description: A Swiss citizen was stopped at the Gandria crossing with two ash parrots without Cites authorization. Intervention by UDSC and USAV.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss citizen stopped at the Gandria border crossing - Transporting two African grey parrots in the car - The animals belong to a protected species - Cites import authorization was missing
## Key facts - Date: Thursday, September 10 - Location: Gandria border crossing - Authorities: FOCBS and FSVO officers - Species: African grey parrots (Appendix I) - Vehicle: Car with Swiss license plates
Officers of the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS) recently intercepted and seized two birds during a routine check at a border crossing. The incident took place on Thursday, September 10, when a Swiss citizen was stopped at the Gandria border crossing while traveling in a car with Swiss license plates. Inside the vehicle, customs officers discovered the presence of two African grey parrots. The driver was in no way in possession of the authorization required by law to import protected specimens. The timely intervention of the border authorities made it possible to block the illegal transport of these particular exotic animals, which fall fully into categories protected at the international level.
### The intervention of customs and veterinary authorities Immediately after the initial check carried out by FOCBS officers, the birds were immediately impounded. The operation took place on the specific order of the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (FSVO). Given the total absence of the documentation required for customs clearance, the two animals were seized with an absolute ban on the owner being able to dispose of them in any way. The competent authorities continue to monitor compliance with customs regulations regarding the transit of protected wildlife species, reminding everyone that every cross-border movement of animals covered by protection agreements must be accompanied by the relevant official permits issued by the designated bodies before travel. ### The owner's statements and the origins of the birds During the checks carried out at the Gandria border crossing, the owner of the two African grey parrots provided his version of the facts to the intervening customs officers. The man stated that he had purchased the birds directly from a private breeder. According to what was reported by the Swiss motorist himself, the seller did not provide him with any Cites certificate at the time of the transfer of the animals. This lack of primary documentation immediately triggered in-depth checks by the FOCBS, as current legislation does not allow exceptions based on the buyer's good faith or the failure to deliver documents by the private seller.
### The species' protection level The owner's situation worsened further due to the particular zoological classification of the transported birds. The African grey parrots in question actually belong to a species listed in Appendix I of protection of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (Cites). This is the highest level of protection provided by the international convention, reserved exclusively for species that are concretely at risk of extinction and whose international trade or transit is strictly regulated and restricted to exceptional and rigorously authorized cases. The total absence of the Cites attestation associated with such a high level of protection explains the firmness with which the FOCBS and the FSVO proceeded with the immediate seizure of the parrots at the border crossing.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Procedures for the transit of protected animals Anyone who needs to transport animals or specimens of protected species across borders must comply with a series of very specific formal procedures established by international conventions and adopted by the federal authorities. Before planning any movement involving customs clearance, it is essential to check the status of the species by consulting the official Cites lists. For animals falling under Annex I, such as the African grey parrots involved in the check at Gandria, it is mandatory to obtain in advance the import and export permits issued by the competent offices. Purchasing from private breeders in no way exempts the buyer from the burden of demanding and verifying the presence of all original documentation before traveling in their own vehicle.
### Tools for customs verification and in-depth analysis To avoid administrative or criminal penalties and the consequent seizure of the animals, it is necessary to regularly consult the directives published by the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (OSAV) and the FOCBS regarding tourist and commercial traffic of goods and protected species. Travelers and commuters who regularly cross customs checkpoints must pay the utmost attention to regulations on the protection of fauna and flora. item.title: Pension Switzerland: Record 725-point Raiffeisen Barometer
item.description: The Raiffeisen and ZHAW barometer reaches the record of 725 points. Pillar 3a grows to 79%, but uncertainty remains over the financing of the AVS.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Raiffeisen and ZHAW barometer at 725 points - First pillar financing and Old Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) among concerns - 39% fear that OASI will not cover expenses - Pillar 3a reaches a new high of 79%
## Key facts - Organization: Raiffeisen and ZHAW - Barometer value: 725 points out of 1000 - Increase: plus 28 points compared to the previous year - Initial value 2018: 587 points - Survey sample: over 1000 people aged between 18 and 65 - OASI concern: 39% of respondents - Pillar 3a share: 79% of the population - Awareness of the new Pillar 3a rule: 63% of the sample - Supplementary contribution: 5% of the sample
The situation of the Swiss pension system is showing further improvement, according to the latest Raiffeisen barometer, produced in collaboration with ZHAW, the Zurich University of Applied Sciences. Driving this progress are primarily the better financial situation of pension funds and a higher savings rate among the population, elements that have directly impacted overall economic conditions. The Risk and Insurance Institute of ZHAW highlighted how economic factors have generated a favorable context. Compared to the previous year, the barometer value rose by twenty-eight points, reaching seven hundred and twenty-five points out of a maximum of one thousand. In the first survey in 2018, the recorded points were five hundred and eighty-seven. This is the highest level since the beginning of the research conducted by the sponsoring entities, signaling a positive dynamic for the Swiss pension system. The overall improvement is primarily due to the good financial conditions of all three pension pillars, but the survey also combines economic indicators with data from a survey conducted on over one thousand people aged between eighteen and sixty-five. This sample provides a picture that highlights not only positive aspects but also persistent elements of uncertainty regarding the future sustainability of the system. The major concern detected among the population remains the long-term financing of the first pillar, with 39% of respondents fearing that OASI will no longer be able to cover its expenses in the future. This data reflects a widespread climate of apprehension among workers regarding the stability of basic public pension benefits in the coming years. In-depth data analysis shows how private pension savings continue to play a central role for resident citizens and for those planning their professional and financial future in Swiss territory, dealing with current rules and regulatory developments concerning occupational pensions and individual provident pillars. Those who wish to delve deeper into retirement planning and understand how contributions work can regularly consult the tools dedicated to [pension planning](nav:pension) to navigate the different pillars of the Swiss system. Alongside fears regarding the financial sustainability of the first pillar and the relevant public institution, data collected by the survey show a growing trend toward voluntary individual pension savings. Increasingly more people are setting aside sums in anticipation of old age, and the share of respondents who own or contribute to a pillar 3a has reached a new high of seventy-nine percent. Further impetus to this form of private savings may have come from the possibility, introduced at the beginning of twenty-twenty-six, to retroactively fill contribution gaps in the third pillar segment. The potential in this regard nevertheless remains broad within the active population. Sixty-three percent are aware of the new rule introduced, but only five percent have actually made a supplementary payment to cover uncovered periods. This discrepancy between the theoretical knowledge of the rule and its concrete application highlights how individual financial planning requires resources and accurate assessments by individual taxpayers. Another aspiration frequently mentioned but particularly difficult to achieve for many workers is early retirement, which often remains a wish rather than a concrete reality. More than half of people aged between fifty-one and sixty-five would like to leave the workforce before the ordinary retirement age, but at the same time almost a third believe they cannot realize this dream due to economic conditions and the requirements necessary to sustain the annuity over time. Financing early retirement will be even more challenging for future generations due to falling conversion rates, higher life expectancy, and increasingly non-linear working careers, as warned by the research institute's experts. Consequently, a potential longer stay in the Swiss professional world also gains greater importance. For about two-thirds of the interviewed sample, working longer would in principle be conceivable, but for most people this option is only viable on a targeted basis or part-time, balancing income needs with the sustainability of work commitment at an advanced age.

item.title: Railway stations in Ticino: decorum and safety
item.description: Question to the Council of State submitted by Daniele Piccaluga of the Ticinese League on the safety and cleanliness of the stations.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Parliamentary question submitted to the Council of State
- Topic: decorum, cleanliness, and safety of railway stations
- Involved hubs: main, regional, and secondary stations
- Coordinated monitoring and SBB plan requested

## Key facts
- Author: Daniele Piccaluga
- Political group: Lega dei Ticinesi
- Cited cases: Bellinzona and Mendrisio
- Involved entities: SBB, Canton, Municipalities, Police

Railway stations in Ticino represent much more than just a transit place for the thousands of commuters who use the connections every day to travel across the region. For tourists and visitors, they constitute the first direct contact with the cities and the canton, effectively acting as a true calling card. For this very reason, it is essential that railway stations—considering both the main hubs located in urban centers and the regional and secondary ones scattered across various areas—manage to guarantee adequate and constant standards of order, cleanliness, decorum, and safety. This is the extreme summary of the official parliamentary question submitted by Daniele Piccaluga, member and coordinator of the Lega dei Ticinesi, to the attention of the Ticino Council of State.

Over the past few months, according to what was highlighted by the Grand Council member, various news reports and numerous testimonies publicly shared by citizens on social media platforms have strongly drawn attention to widespread situations of hardship detected inside railway stations and in the immediately surrounding areas. Among the reported issues are acts of vandalism, presence of filth, damage to structures, individuals harassing travelers in transit, episodes of theft, and various behaviors capable of generating a general sense of insecurity, a perception that tends to intensify particularly during evening hours. The safety of users must not be evaluated solely through objective parameters linked to law enforcement interventions, but requires similar attention toward the perceived safety of those who use public transport on a daily basis.

### The perception of safety among travelers

Students, commuting workers, the elderly, families, and all those people who, especially in the evening, find themselves having to wait alone for a train connection or a bus transfer often express concern in the face of such contexts of degradation. The Ticino deputy specifically recalled the recent cases that occurred at the railway stations of Bellinzona and Mendrisio, episodes that ended up at the center of cantonal media attention, amply demonstrating how the problem deserves careful institutional consideration. Similarly, comparable situations of hardship, acts of vandalism, or critical issues related to safety have been reported over time in other realities present across the cantonal territory, highlighting a trend that is not limited to a single railway station but potentially affects the entire local public transport network. The Swiss Federal Railways themselves, as recalled in the text of the parliamentary question submitted by the representative of the Lega dei Ticinesi, clearly state within their own regulations the primary objective of ensuring stations that are always safe, fully functional, and clean for users. The company's provisions already include precise rules aimed at countering nuisance behavior, acts of vandalism, the uncontrolled dumping of waste, and any other form of degradation that could compromise the usability of collective spaces. The intent of the parliamentary act is certainly not to criminalize certain categories of people, but rather to reaffirm a fundamental and straightforward principle: public spaces intended for collective transport must be able to be used peacefully by all citizens and constantly maintained in decent conditions.
Over recent years, public institutions at various levels have exerted considerable financial and organizational efforts. The Canton, the Confederation, the Municipalities, and transport companies have invested substantial financial resources with the stated objective of enhancing and making regional and national public transport collectively more attractive. In this scenario, it would be profoundly contradictory to decide to increase the frequencies of connections, implement new runs, and proceed with the modernization of material infrastructures without paying the same attention and care to the quality, cleanliness, and security of the physical spaces through which users daily access the mobility network.
### Monitoring of secondary stations
The problem highlighted by the Grand Councillor does not exclusively concern large urban railway stations located in the main centers such as Bellinzona, Lugano, Locarno, Mendrisio, and Chiasso. In secondary and regional stations, especially with the arrival of evening and night hours, the lesser physical presence of railway personnel or on-site surveillance makes the importance of ensuring regular and constant monitoring of the overall conditions of spaces, cleanliness, public lighting, and perceived security levels even more crucial.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). Starting from these premises and detailed considerations, the parliamentary question submits a series of specific questions to the Ticino Government to clarify the true extent of the phenomenon. First, it asks whether the Council of State currently possesses a comprehensive and updated assessment of the situation regarding decorum, cleanliness, and security of all Ticino railway stations, including secondary and peripheral locations. It also inquires what official reports regarding security issues, acts of vandalism, damage, or marked degradation have been received over the last three years by the Cantonal Police or other competent services of the cantonal administration.
A further central aspect concerns the existence or absence of structured and coordinated monitoring among the various institutional and operational actors—namely the Canton, Municipalities, SBB, TILO, Transport Police, and the various cantonal and municipal police forces—aimed at promptly identifying the stations or time slots presenting the greatest critical issues. It is then asked whether the Government currently considers the standards of cleanliness, routine and extraordinary maintenance, night lighting, and surveillance of Ticino stations satisfactory, with a particular emphasis on regional and secondary stations. Finally, clarifications are requested on the procedures by which situations of degradation found by local authorities are reported to SBB and what the average technical intervention times are.
### Requests to the Government and Future Prospects
The final questions posed to the Council of State concern the executive's willingness to formally request SBB to adopt a specific and targeted intervention plan for the Ticino territory, aimed at ensuring adequate, uniform, and homogeneous standards of order, cleanliness, and maintenance in both main and secondary hubs. item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Stefania Filetti elected to the national secretariat of Cgil - A journey that began in the Alfa Romeo factory - Secret ballot by the general assembly gathered in Rome - Ten members in the new confederal secretariat
What: Election to the national secretariat of Cgil Who: Stefania Filetti Where: Rome Organization: Cgil Previous role: General Secretary of Cgil Varese
The general assembly of Cgil, meeting in Rome, elected Stefania Filetti by secret ballot to the organization's new confederal secretariat. The nomination proposal came directly from General Secretary Maurizio Landini, placing Filetti within a renewed team of ten people, evenly divided between five women and five men. This election represents the highest point of a long trade union career that has its roots in Italian industrial departments and has developed through a rigorous path, step by step, without sudden leaps or external accelerations compared to daily groundwork in workplaces.
### From the blue collar to the national secretariat Stefania Filetti's trade union history began in the late 1980s at the Alfa Romeo plant in Arese, a large factory she entered with a work-training contract. This was one of the last generations of workers hired after the factory's transfer to Fiat. Assigned to the mechanics department, Filetti began experiencing the reality of industrial production and the factory every day. It was precisely within that department, in the early 1990s, that she took the first step in her representation activity, becoming a Fiom delegate. This was not an arrival from the outside or from bureaucratic structures, but an experience born directly from the production line and daily contact with the working conditions of her colleagues. Her commitment was consolidated in 1992 with her first official steps as a trade union delegate, laying the groundwork for a gradual transition to roles of greater responsibility within the structure of Fiom Milan, in the historic Sempione area, which took place in 1998 when she became a trade union official. ### Territorial roots in the Varese area Stefania Filetti's journey continues and takes deep roots in the provincial territory starting from 2005, the year she joined the Fiom of Varese. This stage marks a further deepening of the dynamics related to metalworking and local industrial disputes. Two years after her arrival in the Varese structure, she was elected to the metalworkers' secretariat, and then in 2011 she took on the role of general secretary of the category. Here too, her growth took place entirely within the blue-collar category from which her professional and trade union experience had started. Subsequently, her scope of action expanded from the category dimension to the general confederal dimension of the Cgil of Varese. In 2013 she joined the provincial secretariat and in 2018 she assumed the position of organizational secretary, a managerial and political role that allowed her to get to know in detail the complex territorial organization of the organization, including the Chambers of Labour, the trade union offices and the Spi locations.
June 2020 marks another fundamental step with her election as general secretary of the Cgil of Varese, succeeding Umberto Colombo. During the years spent at the head of the Varese Chamber of Labour, Filetti managed a particularly complex period characterized by industrial crises, open trade union disputes, the constant defense of employment and wages, as well as issues related to precariousness and safety in the workplace. In recent years, she has directly addressed the mobilizations promoted by Cgil on referendums concerning work and citizenship, the defense of public healthcare and the protection of workers in contracting out. The approach given to her work finds synthesis in a reflection expressed precisely in 2020: when an idea and a thought become a collective condition shared by the majority, the growth of the common line transforms into authentic trade union militancy. An approach that ideally unites her origins in the factory with the top confederal responsibilities assumed today at the national level.

The uniqueness of this career lies in the absence of shortcuts or level jumps: every role was preceded by hands-on experience in the field, moving from factory worker to union delegate, from official to secretariat member, until holding the position of general secretary of the provincial Fiom first and of the Varese Cgil later. item.title: FFS cargo cuts: Bern responds to Ticino
item.description: The federal government rejects the resolution of the Canton of Ticino on the cuts of FFS Cargo, confirming the management autonomy of the company and the centrality of the north-south axis.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Bern does not intervene on SBB Cargo cuts - The canton's parliamentary resolution rejected - No room for strategic change - Centrality of the north-south corridor confirmed
## Key facts - Questioned: Albert Rösti - Recipient: Daria Lepori - Period of cuts: 2025 and this year - Destination of the letter: President of the Grand Council
The freight traffic landscape along the north-south axis records a clear stance by the federal government regarding the parliamentary resolution submitted to counter the dismantling of SBB Cargo's activities in the Canton of Ticino. Arriving during the summer on the desk of Grand Council President Daria Lepori, the official response signed by the head of the Federal Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications, Albert Rösti, formally closes the door to any corrective intervention by Bern. The federal executive reiterates its firm intention to strictly apply the legal provisions currently in force, maintaining a line of consistency with respect to the framework conditions established at the national level for the transport market. The stance comes following the resolution submitted to the Federal Palace in the month of May, a political act born with the objective of mobilizing central institutions in the face of operational reductions implemented by the Swiss Federal Railways between 2025 and the current year, which first hit the combined transport sector and subsequently that of single wagonload freight. On decisions of an occupational and internal nature to the company, the Federal Council's note is unequivocal, specifying that such choices fall entirely within the management autonomy of SBB, without the government exercising direct influence. The political direction of the Federal Executive toward the transport company materializes solely through the definition of strategic objectives assigned to the owner, while operational management remains entrusted to market dynamics within the general regulatory framework. Despite concerns raised at the cantonal level for the economic and logistical future of the region, the Federal Council expressed satisfaction that no outright layoffs occurred in Ticino, highlighting that the affected staff were able to benefit from internal relocation options, with over half of the workers involved continuing to operate in the rail freight traffic sector.
### The centrality of the transalpine railway line
In the official document transmitted to the Ticino authorities, the central government strongly reiterates that the strategic centrality of the Canton of Ticino along the north-south transit axis remains a fixed point of federal transport policy. However, this territorial confirmation does not translate into a brake on corporate decisions adopted by the railway management. According to what was clarified by the head of the competent federal department, there are no regulatory or political prerequisites for the transport company to back down on the decisions undertaken, nor are there margins for action for the federal government to impose a change in the strategic course undertaken by the railway company. The planning and execution of the operational cuts reflect the structural setup defined by current regulations, leaving unchanged the perimeter of action within which SBB manages its commercial traffic flows and heavy rail transport logistics. The in-depth analysis of the response received from Bern highlights complex dynamics that characterize the relationship between the business choices of large public service companies and the institutional expectations of peripheral or border regions. The stance expressed by the Federal Council highlights a gap between the requests for intervention formulated by local political bodies and the constitutional and legal limits that regulate the action of the central administration regarding former federal monopolies. For economic operators and for those who live and work in the cross-border fabric, these business decisions reflect a profound transformation of the logistics and transport sector, where competitive pressure and the pursuit of economic efficiency end up prevailing over traditional functions of capillary service to the territory. The decision to abandon a binding modal shift objective for domestic freight traffic, decided by parliament during the recent total revision of the freight transport law, demonstrates that the reference legislative framework does not provide specific coercive instruments to force the movement of goods by rail outside of the major trans-Alpine routes. This legislative approach consolidates a market regime in which SBB's business choices enjoy a wide margin of maneuver, aimed at restoring financial health and optimizing operational processes, even when this entails a contraction of regional services linked to single-wagonload freight or proximity combined transport.
### Future scenarios for freight transport and regional logistics
The repercussions of this political and economic orientation extend well beyond the immediate trade union or employment dispute, directly touching the overall logistical architecture of the Ticino territory. The confirmation that current instruments for the promotion of rail freight traffic are considered adequate by the federal government excludes the introduction of new mandates or targeted subsidies to support unprofitable domestic traffic. For Ticino companies that depend on rail freight transport, the panorama outlined by Bern's response imposes a strategic reflection on the supply chain and the need to integrate with the main logistical corridors, accepting a model in which proximity services undergo progressive dismantling in favor of centralized hubs. The transition of personnel, while having avoided mass layoffs thanks to internal relocation measures, still marks a contraction of direct operational presence in the cantonal territory, reducing the capillarity of railway logistics skills available locally. The current situation confirms that the Swiss freight transport market is moving towards greater corporate concentration, leaving cantonal authorities with limited room for maneuver to influence the industrial strategies of a federal company that responds primarily to budget and efficiency constraints established by the owner and by federal public transport laws.

item.title: Because developing new drugs costs more and more
item.description: In 2024, the average cost to develop a new drug reached $2.23 billion, an increase of 65% compared to 2014.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Average drug development cost at $2.23 billion in 2024 - 65% increase compared to 2014, about 25% with inflation - Trump calls for Europe to pay more for new medicines - Zero duties on generics then massive increases according to the administration
## Key facts Development cost 2024: $2.23 billion Increase compared to 2014: 65% in raw percentage Historical comparison: 30% more than in 2012 according to Tufts Oncology weight: 41% of all clinical trials Incidence of rare cancers: 74% of oncology studies started in 2024 Biopharmaceutical companies: 20 largest in the world analyzed by Deloitte
President Donald Trump has repeated it several times: according to him, European governments benefit from US pharmaceutical spending without contributing enough. Higher prices paid in the United States, he says, generate the profits that fund research and innovation from which the rest of the world also benefits. That's why Europe should pay more for new medicines, Trump says. The tenant of the White House reports that customs tariffs remain on standby until 2028, but then they will be 100% for a year and 200% thereafter, as highlighted in a previous in-depth analysis. How true is this statement? The point is difficult to verify, also because the relationship between development costs and drug prices remains one of the most opaque aspects of the pharmaceutical industry. Developing a drug has always been difficult and characterized by a high percentage of clinical failures, but today the nature of the medicines on which global scientific research focuses has also changed. Many new treatments are biologically more complex, and this exponentially increases the costs of research, laboratory work, and industrial production. For decades, many of the best-selling drugs were small chemical molecules, usually taken in the form of pills: statins to lower cholesterol, antidepressants, painkillers like aspirin. Today, companies are moving toward more complex research areas: specialized drugs, gene therapies, and highly specialized treatments for smaller groups of patients, explains Amanda Cole, director at the Office of Health Economics. This category includes, for example, RNA-based therapies, such as mRNA vaccines against Covid-19, cell and gene therapies, and monoclonal antibodies. The latter are proteins produced in the laboratory: they work similarly to natural antibodies and are designed to recognize specific targets. Keytruda, an immunotherapy used in the treatment of certain cancers, is one such key example. These are drugs that can offer great value to patients, but developing them is an extraordinary scientific and economic challenge. For a long time, pharmaceutical innovation focused on parts of the body that scientists knew relatively well, whereas today entirely unprecedented biological frontiers are being explored that require cutting-edge diagnostic tools and technologies. This transition pushes the overall average cost for each single approved drug upward, highlighting how the data in the Deloitte report reflect a structural transformation of the entire international pharmaceutical sector and its related corporate business models.

The increasing complexity of research is also directly reflected in the type of clinical studies needed to obtain regulatory approvals from competent authorities worldwide. According to IQVIA, oncology now accounts for 41% of all clinical trials, and 74% of oncology trials initiated in 2024 evaluated drugs for rare cancers. Finding eligible patients for such targeted trials requires much longer timeframes, global hospital networks, and highly specialized centers. item.title: Mental health and work: absences in Ticino
item.description: 51% of absences for mental reasons lead to the dissolution of the contract. The importance of early intervention for professional stability.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - 51% of absences due to psychological reasons lead to contract termination - 51% of disability insurance (AI) beneficiaries in Ticino suffer from psychiatric disorders - Early intervention increases the chances of retaining one's job - Mental health has become a central issue in the labor market
## Key facts - Percentage of absences leading to contract termination: 51% - Percentage of disability insurance (AI) beneficiaries due to psychiatric reasons: 51% - Percentage of disability insurance (AI) beneficiaries twenty years ago: 33% - Cited source: Compasso
In the context of the Canton Ticino labor market, managing absences related to psychiatric conditions represents a growing challenge for companies and workers, including the numerous cross-border commuters operating in the territory. According to the data, 51% of work absences caused by psychiatric illnesses end in the definitive termination of the employment contract. This figure, analyzed in conjunction with the share of disability insurance (AI) beneficiaries for psychiatric reasons, which is also at 51% in Ticino compared to the 33% recorded just over twenty years ago, outlines a scenario where mental distress heavily impacts professional stability. The issue was placed at the center of a conference organized by Compasso, an organization that deals with professional reintegration, highlighting how absenteeism should be considered a symptom of a pre-existing fragility rather than the main problem. The loss of collaborators, in addition to representing a human cost, translates into a dispersion of skills and experience for Ticino companies.
### The centrality of timely intervention The ability to recognize signs of difficulty before the situation degenerates is crucial to avoid definitive exit from the labor market. As explained by Marzio Proietti, vice president of Compasso, the main risk linked to prolonged absence is that the worker loses contact with the professional environment and the habit of working. The primary objective, also shared by the disability insurance office, is professional reintegration. Monica Maestri Crivelli, head of the Disability Insurance Office, reiterates that the priority is to identify at-risk situations to allow the person to maintain their resources. Timely action by employers not only reduces costs related to absenteeism but protects the human capital within the company, preventing a phase of fragility from turning into a condition of permanent disability. The suggested approach aims at a gradual reintegration that protects both the company, which does not lose the collaborator, and the worker, who maintains their position and income. The analysis of the factors contributing to burnout reveals a complexity that goes beyond simple absence management. In companies operating in the Canton of Ticino, the onset of professional stress conditions is often correlated with structural elements of the work environment. Renato Dotti, president of the Forum Gestione Salute in Azienda, emphasizes how a lack of recognition, difficult relationships with management or colleagues, and the inability to separate private life from work are catalysts for deep distress. The challenge for corporate leadership is not just to manage absences, but to build an environment characterized by psychological safety. This implies the possibility for the worker to express their discomfort or discuss their mistakes without fear of judgment or negative repercussions. Such a preventive approach, based on active listening to employee needs, is essential to prevent the deterioration of mental health.
### Differences between prevention and absence management Overcoming the taboo surrounding mental health is a first step, but translating this awareness into concrete corporate practices remains the real litmus test. For a worker, including the vast number of cross-border commuters who travel daily through border crossings like Brogeda, the awareness that an absence is a warning signal is fundamental. When a prolonged absence occurs, the success rate of reintegration tends to drop drastically over time. Therefore, the management strategy must focus on a gradual return. This path can include trial periods or adapted tasks, which allow the worker to regain confidence and operational capacity without being subjected to excessive pressure. This is an investment that companies must evaluate carefully, considering the cost of losing specialized skills versus the cost of a well-structured reintegration plan. ## In brief - EU proposal for a digital social security passport - Digitalization of diplomas and educational qualifications - Rules that also concern Switzerland
## Key facts - Proposing body: European Commission - Initiative name: European Social Security Pass - Presented to: European Parliament in Strasbourg - Presented by: Roxana Minzatu
The European Commission has put forward a proposal to introduce a continental digital social security passport, known as the European Social Security Pass or Esspass. The initiative, presented to the European Parliament in Strasbourg by European Commission Vice-President Roxana Minzatu, aims to simplify administrative procedures related to cross-border activities for entrepreneurs and facilitate the verification of documents by competent labor inspectorates. In detail, the legislative package provides for the revision of two regulations and also affects Switzerland. When a European Union company carries out work activities in the Confederation, in fact, it is required to take charge of the insurance for posted workers. Currently, the relative certification is issued in paper format, but the adjustment presented in Strasbourg provides that in the future it can also be issued in digital format.
### The European regulatory framework and Swiss involvement Switzerland should adopt the regulatory amendments introduced by the European Union, as they are part of the agreement on the free movement of persons. This was confirmed by an EU official contacted by the Keystone-ATS press agency. The measure is part of a broader package prepared by the European Commission and aimed at ensuring fair labor mobility. In addition to the digital passport, the package includes specific provisions on qualification certificates and the strengthening of the European Labour Authority, the agency established to ensure that rules on the coordination of social security are applied in a simple, effective, and fair manner in all EU Member States. ### The digitalization of diplomas and professional titles Among the new developments presented in Strasbourg is a targeted measure for the digitalization of school and professional documents. Based on the European Commission's proposal, diplomas and educational qualifications must be issued in digital format following uniform standards. This technical evolution aims to simplify and accelerate the document verification procedures by the authorities of another country. Despite the digitalization of formats and the harmonization of standards, the decision regarding the formal recognition of qualifications will still remain the exclusive competence of the national authorities of individual countries. This specific proposal is of direct interest and concrete relevance also for Switzerland, which will have to deal with the new digital standards for educational qualifications in the context of cross-border relations and the movement of professionals.
### The scope of interventions and the institutions involved While the provisions concerning social security and the digitalization of educational qualifications directly affect the Swiss Confederation through the agreement on the free movement of persons, other aspects of the European regulatory package follow different paths. In particular, the strengthening of the European Labour Authority does not concern the Confederation. The aforementioned authority has the specific purpose of supporting the national authorities of member countries and acting as a mediator when disputes arise between the various member states of the European Union. Regarding the institutional process of the presented innovations, the proposals formulated by the EU executive will now have to pass the examination of the European Union legislators, namely the European Parliament and the European Council, before proceeding towards effective adoption and the subsequent phase of transposition by interested third countries, including Switzerland.

item.title: Ticino Plummeting Rentals: 10.9% Decline in Listings
item.description: For the first time, listings in Switzerland are down. In Ticino the decline reaches 10.9% with an average of 1'501 francs.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Decrease in advertised rents in Switzerland by 1.7% - Drop of 10.9% recorded in Ticino - Vacancy rate at 1.92%
- Report date: Sep 15, 2026 - Institute: Swiss Real Estate Institute - Average rent in Ticino: 1,501 francs - Most expensive municipality: Collina d’Oro 2,400 francs - Most affordable municipality: Bodio 990 francs
For the first time since the 2019/20 period, advertised rents in Switzerland recorded an average decrease of 1.7% between July 2025 and the same month in 2026. This analysis emerges from the latest Rental Home Market Price Analysis by the Swiss Real Estate Institute produced for newhome, based on data published on major Swiss real estate portals. The real estate market is going through a phase of profound evolution, where the dynamics between supply and demand are reflected differently depending on the various regions and housing types present across the federal territory.
### The national and regional overview
The most marked decline at the national level is observed in the Canton of Ticino, where advertised rental prices dropped by 10.9%, settling at an average value of 1,501 francs per month. This is followed by the Canton of Zurich with a 3.3% decrease and the Espace Mittelland with a 0.9% reduction. In contrast to these areas, Central Switzerland recorded a rent increase of 2.3%, while Eastern Switzerland marked a 1.4% increase. Zurich firmly confirms itself as the most expensive region in the entire Confederation, with an average monthly net rent of 2,340 francs, while the Espace Mittelland remains the most economical area at 1,452 francs per month for tenants.
Analyzing the Swiss data in detail, the situation highlights marked heterogeneity among the various cantons and different geographical areas. The Lake Lugano area, while remaining the most expensive in Ticino, shows significantly lower values compared to previous periods. Roman Timm, CEO of newhome.ch AG, highlights how today local situations relating to supply and demand are clearly more relevant and heterogeneous compared to national average values, requiring greater attention to individual regional specificities for anyone wishing to understand the dynamics of the current real estate sector. The Ticino real estate market stands out clearly in the Swiss panorama not only for the sharp contraction in advertised prices, but also for the particularity of the data relating to existing properties. The rent for existing properties in Ticino stands at 1,245 francs, making it the lowest among all six regions analyzed nationwide and positioning itself at a level 16% lower than the overall Swiss average. At the same time, the rent for properties on offer exceeds that of existing properties by 17%, highlighting a significant gap between existing lease agreements and new proposals published on real estate portals.
### Variations in municipalities and housing types
The most expensive Ticinese municipalities historically remain those located around Lake Lugano, although current prices are noticeably lower than in the past. Collina d'Oro leads the cantonal ranking with an average value of 2,400 francs, followed by Morcote with 2,300 francs and Paradiso with 1,900 francs. At the opposite end of the ranking, among the most economical municipalities in the Ticino region, Bodio is noted with 990 francs, Balerna with 1,020 francs, and Chiasso with 1,040 francs per month.
The increase in real estate supply has generated a drop in prices in almost all types of municipalities present in Ticino. In peri-urban municipalities, prices recorded a decrease of 13.3%, against an increase in supply of 15.7%. In rural municipalities, the price drop stands at 8.6%, accompanied by a 25.8% increase in listings. The only exception is represented by high-income municipalities, where prices have remained stable thanks to a contraction in supply equal to 13.9%. Regarding housing types, the most consistent drops affect studio apartments at 11.1% and apartments with 5 or more rooms at 10.6%. Three-room apartments, which represent the most widespread type on the market, show a decrease of 7.5% against a 15.7% growth in supply in this specific category. Studio apartments, characterized by a median rent of 800 francs, constitute the most economically accessible housing solution.

Despite the price decreases recorded in recent months, the Canton of Ticino continues to show the highest vacancy rate for apartments in all of Switzerland, standing at 1.92%, a percentage that is almost double the national average of 1.00%. However, the current figure is down compared to the peak reached during 2021, representing a clear sign that the progressive expansion of supply is slowly but steadily absorbing the demand in the Ticino region.
### Investment dynamics and market prospects
The emerging data refutes certain beliefs widespread among economic operators regarding investor strategies. Professor Peter Ilg, director of the Swiss Real Estate Institute, explains how the trend recorded in the Zurich region categorically refutes the idea that owners and investors prefer to keep apartments vacant rather than reduce rents. Over the last three periods examined, an increasing number of real estate listings have been published and, at the same time, rents have decreased. If investors had hoarded apartments, leaving them deliberately vacant, the volume of empty units would have grown even further.
